core: Ways visual art can participate in political communication, commemoration, protest, and institutional power
Propaganda, activist art, public space, circulation, and audience
Evidence-aware interpretation of political claims about artworks
supporting: Print, poster, photograph, mural, installation, and public display
Commission, patronage, censorship, reproduction, and reception
Historical examples from nineteenth-century protest, World War I, Mexican muralism, and Dada

claims.claim: Art can participate in political life through commissions, public display, visual persuasion, criticism, commemoration, protest, and institutional framing, but political meaning must be established for a particular work and context.
Prints and other reproducible media can circulate information and opinion widely because multiplicity, relative cheapness, and ease of production change how an image reaches audiences.

Wartime propaganda used posters, postcards, and trade cards to rally public support, encourage participation, and encourage hostility toward opponents; these functions do not make every political image propaganda.
Artists can use collage, photomontage, satire, public display, and other formal strategies to critique political and cultural norms, as Berlin Dada artists did in the Weimar period and afterward.
A political interpretation should distinguish observable features from documented commission, circulation, reception, or artist statements and from the interpreter's inference.
Public space can be a site of activist action and display; the audience, location, access, and reproduction of a work can alter its political effects and reception.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Political art is often reduced either to direct propaganda or to a claim that every visual form has the same political meaning.
positions: Some works were explicitly commissioned, distributed, or designed to persuade and mobilize audiences.
Other works may criticize, commemorate, document, question, or become politically charged through later display and reception without serving an identical function.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names propaganda as one historically specific mode and asks students to identify medium, sponsor, circulation, audience, and evidence before assigning a political function.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft had no source-grounded distinction among propaganda, protest, circulation, public display, and interpretation.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic language with a historically grounded account of visual art and politics.
Added evidence limits so political readings are not presented as automatic facts.
Added an original public-print scenario and five four-option questions.
rightsIssues: Metropolitan Museum of Art and Smarthistory sources are REFERENCE_ONLY. No images or source prose are reproduced; all lesson prose, scenario, and questions are original.
